results.message: Was Jesus God to your people? Did you believe in the Trinity?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
Was Jesus God to us? Yes - in our own way of saying it. Our teacher called it a sure thing: 'Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light' - a chain of Scripture's own names for him, rather than a philosopher's definition. We confessed the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. 

Did we believe in the Trinity? We answered from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because we held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. 

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea - but our native tongue for that faith was praise.

results.message: What did you believe happens after we die? Do you say everyone outside your faith goes to hell?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
What happens after we die? Our teaching ran through Sheol, the silent country of the dead. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction - and the world's great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling: 'Sin and Hell were terrified: Death trembled and the dead rebelled'. Our poet sang it plainly: 'For our Lord gave His resurrection as a pledge to mortals, that He would remove them from Sheol, which receives the departed without distinction, to the Kingdom which admits the invited with distinction'. What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, we held, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope.

Do we say everyone outside our faith goes to hell? We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts. As for narrowness - one tradition in our own dialogue answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

results.message: Honestly, I doubt my faith a lot. Would your people have had any patience with someone like me?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We would not call what you carry a scandal. Our own word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, our teacher taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. 

What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. Our teacher records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight. 

For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons: 'For all diseases there are medicines, and there will be healing when a skilled physician shall have found them'. A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. What we knew, and what we kept, was faith that is contested, questioned, and still growing.
